title: Choosing long context, managed search, or custom RAG

opening.headline: Learn how to choose between long contexts, managed file search, and build-your-own RAGs based on three criteria: document size, update frequency, and operational burden.
body: If there are 100 documents, I think you can put them all in the prompt. If there are 100,000 documents, it is impossible to insert them at once. The method needs to change somewhere in the meantime, but if you don't have a standard for where to change, you end up creating a search system that is more complicated than necessary, or, conversely, change the method only after you hit a limit.

In this class, we'll look at the architecture of three approaches: a long context where you put the entire document in the prompt, a managed file search where the provider takes care of chunking and indexing, and a build-your-own RAG where you configure the pipeline. Next, we compare the three methods on the same document set and make judgments in two scenarios: 100 documents and 100,000 documents.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the structure of long contexts, managed file searches, and self-built RAGs
You can choose an appropriate method depending on document size, update frequency, and operational burden.

screens.title: As the number of documents increases, how far do you put them and where do you start searching?
screens.lead: First, read about the concerns that arise when document sizes vary. As you read, think about what the baseline might be for changing your approach.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the document stack growing in size in three steps and whether it fits into the context window.

paragraphs: Let's say you're creating an app that answers questions based on in-house documents. If there are 100 documents, I think I can just paste them all into the prompt. However, if there are 100,000 documents, it is impossible to insert them at once. Somewhere between the two extremes, methods must change.

There are three candidates to choose from here. A long context that puts the entire document in the prompt, a managed file search that uploads the file to the provider's tool for chunking and indexing, and a self-built RAG that directly configures chunking, embedding, indexing, and re-ranking.

The problem is that we don't know the standards. If you choose without standards, you will either create a system that is more complicated than necessary, or, conversely, change your approach only after reaching a limit. This class organizes the criteria into three axes: size, frequency of renewal, and operational burden.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: Where is the baseline for moving from long context to search, from managed to self-deployment?

screens.outro: First, let me recall whether, in my experience, the approach has changed depending on scale.

screens.title: Does the method change depending on the size?
screens.lead: Do you use the same method when there are 100 documents and when there are 100,000? When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: If documents change every day, how will your choice of method change?
items.answer: If the document rarely changes, you can prepare it once and use it for a long time, but if it changes every day, the updating process is repeated. If you put it entirely in the prompt, you can just replace the document, but if you build your own search, you have to keep chunking, embedding, and indexing the changed document again. Frequency of renewal is the second criterion.

items.prompt: Do you have the staff to run the search infrastructure yourself?
items.answer: As important as the performance of the method is who operates the method. Indexing, monitoring, and improving search quality are not one-time tasks, but ongoing tasks. If you do not have the manpower to operate it, it is realistic to pass the burden on to the provider. Operational burden is the third criterion.

items.prompt: What questions do we have when we combine the three criteria?
items.answer: These questions include how large the document is in the context window, how often it changes, and who is in charge of operating it. Answering these three questions will most likely narrow down which method is right for you. In the screens that follow, we'll see how each method answers this question.

screens.outro: Now that we have the three criteria in place, let's start with the simplest approach: long context.

screens.title: Long context: Put it all in the prompt
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how far you can fit the entire document into the prompt as it grows.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the context window filling with documents and then overflowing.
labels: Input + Thought + Output share a window

stops.body: The document is much smaller than the context window. The context window is like the model's short-term memory; it can only hold so much at a time. At this size, you can fit all of your documents into the prompt and still have room in the window. Input, thought, and output tokens split the window, leaving space for your answers.

Anthropic advises that if your knowledge base is smaller than 200,000 tokens, or about 500 pages, you can put the entire thing in the prompt without a RAG. At this scale, you don't need to create a search pipeline. If you frequently ask questions using the same document, you can use prompt caching to reduce the delay and cost of repeated questions.

Many of Gemini's models feature large context windows of 1 million tokens or more, allowing for much larger batches of documents. However, just because the window is large, not all questions are efficient. Since each question requires resending large inputs, this should be considered in conjunction with cost-saving measures such as context caching.

If the entire document exceeds the window, you cannot use the whole document method. In this case, a search method is needed that finds only the parts related to the question and adds them to the prompt. Deployment is simplest with long contexts, but from this point on you should move on to managed file retrieval or custom-built RAGs.

screens.outro: Since search is needed at scales beyond windows, we will compare two branches of search approaches.

screens.title: Managed File Search and Build Your Own RAG
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the structure of both search methods. RAG finds relevant information from the knowledge base and appends it to the prompt.

visual.alt: A two-line structure diagram comparing who is responsible for which steps in managed file search and direct deployment RAG.

tabs.label: Managed File Search
tabs.body:
This is a method where the provider receives the file and takes care of chunking and indexing. Gemini File Search takes your data, chunks it, and indexes it. OpenAI's file search finds files uploaded to the vector store through semantic search and keyword search. When you add files to the vector store, they are automatically chunked, embedded, and indexed.

I don't need to implement tool execution in my code, the model just calls the tool when needed. Instead, the room for chunking or reranking is less than building directly.

tabs.label: Build your own RAG
tabs.body:
RAG is constructed in the following order: The knowledge base is divided into chunks, usually no more than a few hundred tokens, and an embedding model converts each chunk into a meaningful vector and stores it in a vector database. When a query comes in, the most relevant chunk is found based on semantic similarity and added to the prompt.

I decide the chunking criteria, embedding model, index, and re-ranking, so I can fine-tune them. To that extent, I have to manage all of the index updates, monitoring, and quality improvement.

tabs.label: Improve search quality
tabs.body:
A problem we often run into with manual builds is that context is lost when we look at just one chunk. For example, the chunk that says a company's sales increased 3% over the previous quarter doesn't know which company or which quarter it is from.

Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval is a method of creating embeddings and BM25 indexes by prepending descriptive context to each chunk. This method reduced search failures by 49%, and when combined with re-ranking, it reduced them by 67%. This is an example of the room for adjustment that building your own gives you.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the structure of the two methods, we will compare the three methods at a glance by substituting them in the same document set.

data.notes: The cost structure varies depending on the method. Gemini File Search is free for storing files and creating embeddings at query time, and only costs embedding costs and model input/output token costs at the time of initial indexing. Operational burdens include who is responsible for updating the index, monitoring, and improving search quality. The three columns of the table are not about superiority or inferiority, but rather options tailored to different conditions, so read them in order to narrow down the columns by first looking at size, then renewal and operational burden.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the criteria into a comparison table, let's apply them to the two scenarios.

screens.title: Scenario A: 100 documents
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of selecting a method based on three criteria under the condition that there are 100 documents. Select the right arrow to check the basis for judgment one by one.

steps.title: condition
steps.body: There are 100 documents, totaling less than a few hundred thousand tokens. Renewal is only once a month. You must choose a method under these conditions.

steps.title: Step 1: Estimate total tokens
steps.body: First, we estimate the number of tokens throughout the document and compare them to the context window. The idea is to check whether the length of one document multiplied by 100 fits into the window. Rather than guessing from the number of characters or pages, it is more accurate to actually count the tokens. At this time, the tokens for answers and thoughts share the same window, so if the document almost fills the window, there is not enough space.

steps.title: Step 2: Once in the window, insert the whole thing.
steps.body: If you enter a window, place the entire document in the prompt. Because questions are repetitive, we also use prompt caching to reduce repetition costs. There is no need for chunking, embedding, or indexing.

steps.title: Step 3: Update ends with document replacement
steps.body: Once a month, if your documents change, you can simply replace the document you put in the prompt. Updates are simple as there is no need to recreate the index. There is no need to worry about whether to change the chunking standard or the embedding model.

steps.title: Step 4: Why has the lowest operational burden?
steps.body: Since there is no search system, there are few places to check. If your scale is small and updates are rare, it becomes clear why you would choose the long context with the lowest operational burden. It is never too late to introduce complex approaches when scale demands.

steps.title: Signs of change in choice
steps.body: If your documents are too large to fit in the window, or the cost and delay of sending large inputs for each question becomes burdensome, it's time to move to a search method. If you determine this signal in advance, you can move on to the next method without panic when the system grows.

screens.outro: Now let’s judge by the same criteria in Scenario B, which is on a significantly different scale.

screens.title: Scenario B: 100,000 documents
screens.lead: The same criteria applies to the condition where there are 100,000 documents. Select the right arrow to see where your choice diverges from Scenario A.

steps.title: condition
steps.body: There are 100,000 documents and they are updated daily. There is no one on the team responsible for search infrastructure.

steps.title: Step 1: Can't put it in a window
steps.body: 100,000 won't fit into the context window. At this point we diverge from Scenario A. You need to search to find only the relevant parts and put them into the prompt.

steps.title: Step 2: If you do not have operational personnel, start with management type
steps.body: Manually indexing large volumes of documents that are updated daily requires staff to handle updates, monitoring, and quality improvement. If you are not in charge, start with managed file search, where chunking and indexing are handled by the provider.

steps.title: Step 3: If insufficient, adjust manually
steps.body: If the quality of managed search isn't up to par, it then moves on to RAG, which directly coordinates chunking and re-ranking. This must be weighed against workforce planning to ensure that operational burden is taken on at the expense of room for adjustment.

steps.title: The dividing point between A and B
steps.body: Scenario A ended up with a long context where the scale went inside the window, while B ended up with a search where the scale went beyond the window. After that, the operations staff split between managed and direct deployment. Scale, renewal and operational burden change the way we do it.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the criteria with the two scenarios, we will conclude by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: The criteria for determining the method are the size of the document, frequency of update, and operational burden. If a document enters the context window, it is placed in its entirety as a long context. If it goes beyond the window, a search is required. If the operational staff is burdened, a managed file search is used first.

Build-your-own RAGs have the greatest room for quality improvement, with chunking, embedding, indexing, and re-ranking all adjustable, but they also have the greatest operational burden. Rather than choosing a complicated method from the beginning, it is safer to start with a simple method and move on when you see limitations.

No matter how many documents you have, you can put them all in the prompt.
Low operational burden as index and tool execution are not directly implemented

checks.explain: The managed type imports files, takes care of chunking and indexing, and calls the model when needed, so the operational burden is low. Instead, the room for adjustment is less than building it yourself.

wrong.0: The ones that allow for fine-tuning are the self-built RAGs, which come at the cost of high operational burden.
wrong.1: The method of inserting the entire document is a long context, and cannot be used if the document exceeds the window.
wrong.3: There is no evidence that the managed type always produces better quality, and if quality is lacking, it goes to RAG, which directly adjusts.

glossary.def: This involves putting the entire document in a prompt and having the model read it at once.
It is a tool that takes care of chunking, indexing, and searching by the provider and calls the model when it is needed.
I configure chunking, embedding, indexing, and re-ranking to find relevant information and add it to the prompt.
It involves dividing a document into small pieces that become search units.
This is the manpower and time required to update the index, monitor, and improve search quality.

misconceptions.myth: If the context window is large, RAG is not necessary.
misconceptions.fact: At scale beyond the window or with frequent updates, search is still required. A simple solution is to put the whole thing in just the size that fits into the window.

misconceptions.myth: If it is a managed type, there is nothing to configure.
misconceptions.fact: It's still up to me to upload files, declare search tools, and check search quality. What is reduced is implementation overhead such as chunking and indexing.

misconceptions.myth: A self-built RAG is always more accurate.
misconceptions.fact: More room for adjustment does not automatically mean it is more accurate. Because the operational burden is also large, it is chosen when the quality of the managed type is insufficient.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Size, frequency of renewal, and operational burden determine the method.
Small scales require long context, and scales beyond the window require searching.
If there is a shortage of operational personnel, use managed search first.
When more fine-tuning is needed, go directly to the Build RAG.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of the three approaches is closest to the size and frequency of updates of my documents?
